content: Uterine fibroids, also known as leiomyomas, fibromyomas, or simply fibroids, are benign (non-cancerous) tumors that develop in the uterus, a key organ in the female reproductive system. Symptoms of Uterine Fibroids: Women with uterine fibroids may experience a sensation of abdominal fullness, bloating, or constipation. Bleeding between menstrual periods is a common symptom. An increase in urinary frequency may occur due to pressure on the bladder. Heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) is often reported, sometimes accompanied by the passage of blood clots. Menstrual periods may last longer than usual. Pelvic cramping or pain during menstruation is another frequent complaint. A feeling of fullness or pressure in the lower abdomen is common. Pain during sexual intercourse may also be experienced. Causes of Uterine Fibroids: Uterine fibroids are the most common type of pelvic tumor. They are present in approximately 20% of women during their childbearing years (from the onset of menstruation until menopause). Fibroids are more frequently observed in women over the age of 30 and are rare in women under 20. They often shrink and become asymptomatic after menopause. African American women are more likely to develop fibroids compared to Caucasian women. The exact cause of fibroids is unknown, but their growth appears to be influenced by the hormone estrogen. As long as a woman is menstruating, fibroids are likely to grow, albeit usually at a slow rate. Fibroids can vary greatly in size, ranging from microscopic to large masses that can fill the entire uterus and weigh several pounds. While a single fibroid can develop, it is more common for multiple fibroids to be present. Fibroids are classified based on their location in the uterus: Myometrial: Located within the muscular wall of the uterus. Submucosal: Found just beneath the uterine lining. Subserosal: Situated just beneath the outer covering of the uterus. Pedunculated: Attached to the uterus by a stalk, either on the outer surface or within the uterine cavity. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: Contact your healthcare provider if you notice gradual changes in your menstrual pattern, such as heavier bleeding, increased cramping, or bleeding between periods. Seek medical attention if you develop a sensation of fullness or heaviness in your lower abdomen. Diagnosis: A pelvic examination may reveal an irregularly shaped, enlarged, or lumpy uterus, which is often sufficient for diagnosis. In some cases, diagnosing fibroids can be challenging, particularly in obese women. Fibroids may be mistaken for: Pregnancy Ovarian tumors Inflammation of the fallopian tubes Uterine adenomyosis (a condition where the uterine lining grows into the muscle wall of the uterus) Imaging studies such as transvaginal or pelvic ultrasound are commonly used to confirm the diagnosis. In some cases, a pelvic MRI may be necessary. An endometrial biopsy (sampling of the uterine lining) or laparoscopy may be performed to rule out cancer. Treatment Options: Treatment depends on several factors, including the patient’s age, overall health, severity of symptoms, type of fibroids, pregnancy status, and future fertility goals. Options include: 1. Monitoring: Some women may only require periodic pelvic exams or ultrasounds to monitor fibroid growth. 2. Symptom Management: Oral contraceptives: Birth control pills can help control heavy menstrual bleeding. Hormonal IUDs: Devices that release progestin can reduce heavy bleeding and pain. Iron supplements: Used to prevent or treat anemia caused by heavy periods. NSAIDs: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs like ibuprofen or naproxen can alleviate cramps and pain. Hormonal therapy: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists or Depo Leuprolide injections may shrink fibroids temporarily. These are typically used before surgery or for women nearing menopause. Side effects include hot flashes and vaginal dryness. 3. Surgical and Procedural Interventions: Hysteroscopic resection: For fibroids growing inside the uterine cavity, this outpatient procedure involves inserting a small camera and instruments through the cervix to remove the fibroids. Uterine artery embolization: This procedure cuts off the blood supply to the fibroid, causing it to shrink and die. Women considering future pregnancies should discuss this option with their healthcare provider. Myomectomy: This surgery removes fibroids while preserving the uterus, making it a preferred option for women who wish to maintain fertility. However, new fibroids may develop after the procedure. Hysterectomy: This invasive surgery involves removing the uterus and is considered when other treatments fail or are not viable. Prognosis: Many women with fibroids are asymptomatic and may not require treatment. During pregnancy, fibroids may grow due to increased blood flow and estrogen levels but typically return to their original size after delivery. Possible Complications: Fibroids can lead to pregnancy complications, though the risk is generally low: Most women can carry their pregnancies to term, but some may deliver prematurely due to limited space in the uterus. In some cases, fibroids may block the birth canal or cause the baby to be positioned incorrectly, necessitating a cesarean section. Heavy bleeding immediately after childbirth is another potential complication for women with fibroids.
